## REPO-009 — Statically audit GitHub Actions workflows (zizmor) for injection, over-broad permissions, persisted credentials and unpinned actions

**What.** zizmor runs as a pre-commit hook (and thus in CI via
`just hooks`, REPO-007) against every workflow file (plus
`.github/dependabot.yml`, `action.yml` and `.pre-commit-{config,hooks}.yaml`), flagging
template-injection, over-broad `permissions:`, persisted credentials, and
unpinned actions.

**Why.** These are exactly the classes of GitHub Actions vulnerabilities
that show up in real supply-chain incidents (a workflow that interpolates
untrusted `${{ }}` input into a shell step, a token with more scope than
the job needs, a checkout step that leaves credentials persisted for a
later malicious step to exfiltrate). Catching them statically, before
merge, is cheaper than an incident review.
Source: https://docs.zizmor.sh/

> `zizmor` is a static analysis tool for your CI/CD.
> It can find and fix security issues in common CI/CD setups,
> including GitHub Actions, Dependabot, and pre-commit.

**How.** In `.pre-commit-config.yaml` (REPO-001):

```yaml
  # Static analysis of the workflows themselves: template injection, over-broad permissions,
  # credential persistence, unpinned actions.
  - repo: https://github.com/zizmorcore/zizmor-pre-commit
    rev: c92afdf2c6ca336aaa8f39e2bd8d48f62dbd8e1f  # frozen: v1.31.1
    hooks:
      - id: zizmor
```

The findings it raises map to fixes like these in the workflow:

```yaml
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1  # v7.0.1 — full-SHA pin
        with:
          persist-credentials: false  # nothing here pushes; don't leave a token in .git/config
      - run: uv run --frozen just smoke-example "$EXAMPLE"
        env:
          EXAMPLE: ${{ matrix.example }}  # via env, never interpolated into the script
```

**When NOT to apply.** A repo with no `.github/workflows/` (no CI at all)
has nothing for zizmor to audit; a repo whose workflows are all generated
and reviewed by a platform team upstream may run this audit there instead
of per-repo.

## REPO-010 — Workflows start from `permissions: {}` and each job requests only the `GITHUB_TOKEN` scopes it needs

**What.** Workflow-level `permissions: {}` removes every default scope;
each job then declares exactly what it needs (for example
`contents: read`).

**Why.** The token's default scopes can be broad, and every step,
third-party actions included, can use the token. Starting from nothing
means a compromised or buggy step can do only what that job was
explicitly granted.
Source: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use.md

> It's good security practice to set the default permission for the `GITHUB_TOKEN` to read access only for repository contents. The permissions can then be increased, as required, for individual jobs within the workflow file.

**How.**

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

# Least privilege: nothing by default; each job asks for exactly what it needs.
permissions: {}

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions:
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1  # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@c18668ad3cf93ea998bef934396af7bb5c839dc7  # v10.2.0
      - run: uv sync --locked
      - run: uv run --frozen just test
```

**When NOT to apply.** Never skip it; a job that genuinely needs write
access (a release, a PR comment) declares that one scope on that one job.

## REPO-011 — Lock workflow dependencies in `.github/workflows/actions.lock` and verify it in CI

**Requires.** gh-actions-lock>=0.2 (preview)

**What.** Generate a workflow dependency lockfile with the
`gh actions-lock` CLI extension and commit it. It pins every action your
workflows use, transitive actions included, to a commit SHA and records
the source repository's numeric identity. A CI job runs
`gh actions-lock --verify` on every pull request, and CODEOWNERS
(REPO-008) owns the lockfile. The feature is in public preview.

**Why.** A tag such as `@v3` resolves to whatever commit it points at
when the job runs; if a maintainer account is compromised and the tag is
repointed, your CI runs the new code. Full-SHA pins (REPO-009) fix that
only for direct references and only where someone wrote them. The
lockfile also covers actions your actions call, and the runner checks
the locked commit and repository identity at job start.
Source: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/security/workflow-dependency-lockfiles.md

> A workflow dependency lockfile pins a commit SHA to every action (including transitive dependencies) and reusable workflow your workflows depend on.

**How.**

```bash
gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock
gh actions-lock      # pin every resolvable action; rerun after changing any `uses:`
git add .github/workflows/
```

```yaml
# .github/workflows/verify-lockfile.yml: fails when actions.lock is stale or a pin no longer verifies
jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    permissions:
      contents: read
    env:
      GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1  # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock --pin v0.4.0
      - run: gh actions-lock --verify
```

Dependabot (REPO-002) regenerates the matching lockfile entry in its own
action bumps. Never edit `actions.lock` by hand. For a commit-time check,
`gh actions-lock --verify-local --no-fix` is offline but checks coverage
only, not provenance. Once every workflow is onboarded, the **Require
lockfile** policy blocks runs of targeted workflows that aren't.

**When NOT to apply.** GitHub Enterprise Server, which the extension
doesn't support. While the feature is in preview, keep REPO-009's
full-SHA pins as well. The lockfile doesn't lock reusable workflows
called from another repository (that repository's own lockfile covers
them) or container images.

## REPO-013 — Turn on CodeQL code scanning with default setup

**What.** Enable CodeQL **default setup** (Settings → Advanced Security →
CodeQL analysis → Set up → Default). With no workflow file to maintain,
it scans the default branch and protected branches on push, pull
requests against them, and runs a weekly scan. It picks up new CodeQL
languages, GitHub Actions workflows included, automatically.

**Why.** Secret scanning (REPO-004, REPO-012) finds credentials, not
vulnerable code; zizmor (REPO-009) audits only workflows. Without code
scanning, an injection or path-traversal bug in the code itself has no
gate before merge. Default setup is free for public repositories; private
and internal ones need GitHub Code Security.
Source: https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/find-and-fix-code-vulnerabilities/configure-code-scanning/configure-code-scanning.md

> We recommend that you start using code scanning with default setup.

**How.**

```bash
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/code-scanning/default-setup              # "state": "not-configured" | "configured"
gh api -X PATCH repos/OWNER/REPO/code-scanning/default-setup -f state=configured
```

**When NOT to apply.** Repositories that need a custom build for a
compiled language, a matrix or a different schedule use advanced setup (a
CodeQL workflow) instead; switching to default setup disables that
workflow. Repositories with no CodeQL-supported language gain nothing,
though enabling it there costs no Actions minutes.

## REPO-016 — Pin `runs-on` to a versioned runner image, not `-latest`

**What.** Write `runs-on: ubuntu-24.04` (or the `macos-`/`windows-`
equivalent) instead of `ubuntu-latest`. Move the pin in a reviewed PR,
before the image is deprecated.

**Why.** `-latest` is a moving label. The runner-images README: "The
`-latest` migration process is gradual and happens over 1-2 months" and
"During this process, any workflow using the `-latest` label, may see
changes in the OS version", so the same commit can pass on one run and
fail on the next after a distro, glibc or preinstalled-tool bump, with no
diff to blame. The same page says "To avoid unwanted migration, users can
specify a specific OS version in the yaml file". On 2026-11-25,
`ubuntu-latest` is Ubuntu 26.04 while many workflows were written for
24.04.

**How.**

```yaml
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04   # bump deliberately when the image nears deprecation
```

**When NOT to apply.** Jobs that exist to test against the newest OS
(a canary job on `-latest` is fine), or a job that only runs a container
image where the host OS does not matter. Pinned images are deprecated
too ("we only support the latest 2 versions of an OS"), so schedule the
bump.

## REPO-017 — Cancel superseded CI runs with `concurrency` and `cancel-in-progress`

**What.** In a CI workflow triggered by `pull_request` or pushes to
topic branches, add a workflow-level `concurrency` group keyed on the
workflow and the ref, with `cancel-in-progress: true`.

**Why.** Without it, every push to a PR starts a full run on a commit
that is already stale. They all keep running and queue behind each
other, so the run that matters waits and hosted minutes are spent on
results no one reads. GitHub: "Use `concurrency` to ensure that only a
single job or workflow using the same concurrency group will run at a
time", and "To also cancel any currently running job or workflow in the
same concurrency group, specify `cancel-in-progress: true`."

**How.**

```yaml
concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  # cancel only PR runs; main keeps every run
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
```

**When NOT to apply.** Never cancel runs on the default branch (a
cancelled run leaves a commit with no result), tag/release workflows,
deploys or migrations (a cancel mid-deploy leaves a half-applied
change); give those a group without `cancel-in-progress`, so they queue.
Note a group keeps at most one pending run, so a third push replaces the
pending second run (docs: "any existing `pending` job or workflow in the
same concurrency group will be canceled").

---

## REPO-018 — Set `timeout-minutes` on every job

**What.** Give each job an explicit `timeout-minutes`, about 2-3 times its
normal duration, so a stuck job fails fast.

**Why.** The default is "360" ("The maximum number of minutes to let a
job run before GitHub automatically cancels it. Default: 360"). A test
that deadlocks or a download that never returns holds the runner, and any
concurrency group slot (REPO-017), for up to 6 hours, burns billed
minutes, and shows as "running" instead of failing.

**How.**

```yaml
jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    timeout-minutes: 15
```

**When NOT to apply.** Never omit it. Jobs that legitimately run for
hours (large builds, long soak tests) get a ceiling above their normal
runtime, not the default. A step-level `timeout-minutes` covers one
unreliable step.
